The map fk can be considered as a refinement of Euler's phi function. For example, we may define another map gk: Z -> Z where gk(m) = phi(m) = k, i.e. the map mapping all m to their totient value. The image of gk is obviously the singleton {k}; gk is trivially surjective, and Carmichael's conjecture is that it is never injective. Since the image of fk contains those unit groups (Z/mZ)* such that |(Z/mZ)*| = k, f_k exhibits richer mapping properties.

A401163: Primes p such that, considering only splits containing at least one composite segment, the set of terminal primes reachable along

The process: Given a prime p, consider all ways to split its decimal representation into consecutive segments such that (i) no segment equals 1, (ii) no segment has a leading zero, and (iii) at least one segment is composite. For each such split, replace every composite segment by its prime factors in ascending order, then concatenate all resulting primes, preserving the original order of segments. If the concatenated number is prime, the process terminates; otherwise, repeat the splitting on the new number. A terminal prime is a prime at which the process terminates. It is conjectured that every prime eventually terminates.

The Mathar conjecture is true. Generally from the factorial form, the last term is the "extra" product beyond the prior term, from k=n-1 and 3k+2 evaluates to 3*(n-1)+2 = 3n-1, yielding a(n) = a(n-1)*(3n-1) (eqn1). Similarly, a(n) = a(n-2)*(3n-1)*(3(n-2)+2) = a(n-2)*(3n-1)*(3n-4) (eqn2) and a(n) = a(n-3)*(3n-1)*(3n-4)*(3*(n-2)+2) = a(n-3)*(3n-1)*(3n-4)*(3n-7) (eqn3). We equate (eqn2) and (eqn3) to get a(n-2)*(3n-1)*(3n-4) = a(n-3)*(3n-1)*(3n-4)*(3n-7) or a(n-2)+(7-3n)*a(n-3) = 0 (eqn4). From (eqn1) we have a(n)+(1-3n)*a(n-1) = 0 (eqn5). Combining (eqn4) and (eqn5) yields a(n)+(1-3n)*a(n-1)+a(n-2)+(7-3n)*a(n-3) = 0.

From Peter Bala, Nov 14 2022: a(n) = A000032(5^n). a(n) = a(n-1)^5 + 5*a(n-1)^3 + 5*a(n-1) with a(1) = 11. a(n) == 1 (mod 5). a(n+1) == a(n) (mod 5^(n+1)) for n >= 1 (a particular case of the Gauss congruences for the Lucas numbers). Coordination sequence for Dual(3^3.4^2) tiling with respect to a tetravalent node. This tiling is also called the prismatic pentagonal tiling, or the cem-d net. It is one of the 11 Laves tilings. (The identification of this coordination sequence with the g.f. in the definition was first conjectured by Colin Barker, Jan 22 2018.) · a(n) = a(n-1) + a(n-3) - a(n-4) for n>4. There is a conjecture arising in Sequence Machine that a(n) = A026491(2+n)-1. This appears to be true: Here we start from on odious or evil number and apply a minimum number of van-Eck-Transforms (of A171898) to reach a value larger than a(n-1). The Dekking formula in A026491 says that A026491 is essentially a partial sum of the backward van-Eck-Transforms, and in a (vague) manner this seems to match.

This same problem is described in a different but equivalent way in A140100 and A140101. See A140101 for a conjectured recurrence which underlies all these sequences. - N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 28-30, 2016

Let M = [[0,0,1], [0,1,1], [1,1,1]], X(n) = M^(n-2), and Y(n) = M^(floor(n/2)-2) = X(floor(n/2)) (with negative powers indicating matrix inverses). Let also, t1 = [1,1,1]^T, t2 = [1,2,2]^T, and t3 = [1,2,3]^T. In addition, define b(n) = (1/2)*(t1^T X(n) t1) and c(n) = (1/2)*(t3^T Y(n) t1) if n is even and = (1/2)*(t2^T Y(n) t1) if n is odd. From Antti Karttunen, Jul 31 - Aug 06 2020: As a curiosity, like with sigma, also here a(14) = a(15). [Cf. also A003973 and A341512] Question: is it possible that a(k) = 2*k for any k? If not, then the deficiency (A033879) cannot be -1, and there are no quasiperfect numbers. If there were such cases, then A156552(k) = q would be an instance of quasiperfect number, which should also be an odd square, thus k would need to be of the form 4u+2. In range n <= 10000, a(n) is a nontrivial multiple of n only at n = [25, 35, 343, 539, 847, 3315] with a(n) = [125, 105, 2401, 2695, 2541, 9945]. The quotients are thus also odd: 5, 3, 7, 5, 3, 3. From Robert Israel, Feb 25 2019: 2*n^3/5 + 3/(2*n) > 1/{(10+n^4)^(1/4)} > 2*n^3/5 for all n. From this we can show that a(5*k) = 50*k^3 for k >= 1, a(5*k+1) = 50*k^3 + 30*k^2 + 6*k for k >= 1, a(5*k+2) = 50*k^3 + 60*k^2 + 24*k + 3, a(5*k+3) = 50*k^3 + 90*k^2 + 54*k + 10 for k >= 1, a(5*k+4) = 50*k^3 + 120*k^2 + 96*k + 25. This implies the conjectured recurrence for n >= 12.

From Peter Bala, Jul 24 2012: T(n,k) = sum {j=0..k}(-1)^(k-j)/4^j*C(n+1/2,k-j)*C(2*j,j)*(2*j+1)^n. Recurrence equation: T(n+1,k) = (2*k+1)*T(n,k) + 2*(n-k+1)*T(n,k-1). E.g.f.: sqrt(E(x,2*z)) = 1 + z + (1+2*x)*z^2/2! + (1+10*x+4*x^2)*z^3/3! + ..., where E(x,z) = (1-x)/(exp(z*(x-1)) - x) is the e.g.f. for the Eulerian numbers (version A173018). Cf. A156919. Row polynomial R(n,x) = sum {k = 1..n} 2^(n-2*k)*C(2*k,k)*k!*Stirling2(n,k)*(x-1)^(n-k). R(n,4*x)/(1-4*x)^(n+1/2) = sum {k>=0} C(2*k,k)*(2*k+1)^n*x^k. The sequence of rational functions x*R(n,x)/(1-x)^(n+1) conjecturally occurs in the first column of (I - x*A112857)^(-1). (1+x)^(n-1)*R(n,x/(x+1)) gives the n-th row polynomial of A186695. A211433: Number of ordered triples (w,x,y) with all terms in {-n,...,0,...,n} and w+2x+4y=0.

Also, a(n) is the number of ordered pairs (w,x) with both terms in {-n,...,0,...,n} and w+2x divisible by 4. If (w,x) is such a pair it is easy to see that (-w,x), (-w,-x), and (w,-x) also are such pairs. The number of pairs with both w and x positive is given by A211521(n). If w=0, x must be even, and if x=0, w must be divisible by 4. This means that a(n) = 4*A211521(n) + 2*floor(n/2) + 2*floor(n/4) + 1. Since the sequences A211521(n), floor(n/2), floor(n/4), and the constant sequence all satisfy the recurrence conjectured in the formula section, a(n) must also satisfy the recurrence, so this proves the conjecture. · Conjectures from Colin Barker, May 15 2017: G.f.: (1 + 5*x^2 + 4*x^3 + 5*x^4 + x^6) / ((1 - x)^3*(1 + x)^2*(1 + x^2)). a(n) = a(n-1) + a(n-2) - a(n-3) + a(n-4) - a(n-5) - a(n-6) + a(n-7) for n>6.

If (w,x) is such a pair it is easy to see that (-x,w), (-w,-x), and (x,-w) also are such pairs. If both w and x are nonzero these four pairs lie one in each quadrant. If one of w or x is zero, the other must be a multiple of 5. This means that a(n) equals 4*A211523(n) (the nonzero pairs) plus 4*floor(n/5) + 1 (pairs with w or x equal to zero). From Chai Wah Wu, May 28 2018: The following are all conjectures. For m >= 0, the 2^(m+1)-th row are the figurate numbers based on the 2^m-dimensional regular convex polytope with g.f.: (1+x)^(2^m-1)/(1-x)^(2^m+1). From Peter Bala, Jul 08 2022: Conjecture: Let k be a positive integer. The sequence obtained by reducing a(n) modulo k is eventually periodic with the period dividing phi(k) = A000010(k). For example, modulo 16 we obtain the sequence [1, 1, 3, 3, 7, 3, 15, 11, 7, 3, 15, 11, 7, 3, 15, 11, ...], with an apparent period of 4 beginning at a(4). Cf. A167137. More generally, we conjecture that the same property holds for integer sequences having an e.g.f. of the form G(exp(x) - 1), where G(x) is an integral power series.

The Shannon (zero-error) capacity of a graph G is Θ(G) = lim_k α(G^⊠k)^{1/k}, where α is the independence number and ⊠ the strong product. Determine Θ(C₇) (and Θ(C_{2k+1}) for every odd cycle of length at least 7). Lovász (1979) proved Θ(C₅) = √5 with his theta function; for C₇ the best bounds are 367^{1/5} ≈ 3.2578 ≤ Θ(C₇) ≤ ϑ(C₇) = 7cos(π/7)/(1+cos(π/7)) ≈ 3.3177 (lower bound: an independent set of size 367 in C₇^⊠5, Polak–Schrijver 2019).

Let X be uniform on {0,1}ⁿ and Y the output of a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability α ∈ (0, 1/2) applied to each coordinate of X. Conjecture: every Boolean function f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1} satisfies I(f(X); Y) ≤ 1 − h(α), where h is the binary entropy function; dictator functions f(x) = xᵢ attain it. Known in the high-noise regime (α close to 1/2, Samorodnitsky 2016); open in general.
Capacity of the binary deletion channel

The binary deletion channel deletes each input bit independently with probability d ∈ (0,1) and outputs the surviving bits in order, without revealing which positions were deleted. Determine its capacity C(d) (which exists, by Dobrushin) for any d ∈ (0,1): no closed form, single-letter characterization or matching bounds are known for any interior d. Known: C(d) = 1 + d log₂ d − O(d) as d → 0 (Kanoria–Montanari), and C(d) = Θ(1 − d) as d → 1, with a constant-factor gap between the explicit bounds.
Entropy region of four or more random variables

For jointly distributed discrete random variables X₁,…,Xₙ, the vector of the 2ⁿ − 1 joint entropies H(X_S), ∅ ≠ S ⊆ {1,…,n}, is called entropic; the closure Γ̄*ₙ of the set of entropic vectors is a convex cone. Characterize Γ̄*ₙ explicitly for n ≥ 4. For n ≤ 3 it is exactly the cone cut out by the Shannon inequalities; for n = 4 it is strictly smaller (Zhang–Yeung 1998, the first non-Shannon inequality) and is not polyhedral (Matúš 2007), so no finite list of linear inequalities describes it.
Capacity region of the two-receiver broadcast channel

One sender encodes two independent messages into an input sequence Xⁿ of a discrete memoryless broadcast channel p(y₁, y₂ | x); receiver i must decode message i from Yᵢⁿ. Find a single-letter (computable) characterization of the capacity region for a general channel. Posed by Cover (1972). Solved for degraded, less noisy and more capable channels and for the Gaussian MIMO broadcast channel; Marton's inner bound (1979) is not known to be strictly smaller than capacity for any channel, and whether it is the capacity region is itself open.

A relay channel p(y, y_r | x, x_r) has a sender X, a receiver observing Y, and a relay that observes Y_r and transmits X_r, each relay symbol depending only on its past observations. Determine the capacity of the general discrete memoryless relay channel by a single-letter formula (the Gaussian case with fixed gains is already open). Posed by van der Meulen (1971). Known for degraded, reversely degraded and semideterministic relay channels (Cover–El Gamal 1979; El Gamal–Aref 1982); the cutset bound is not tight in general.
Capacity region of the two-user Gaussian interference channel

Two senders and two receivers: Y₁ = X₁ + aX₂ + Z₁ and Y₂ = bX₁ + X₂ + Z₂, with independent standard Gaussian noise and average power constraints P₁, P₂; receiver i decodes only sender i's message. Determine the capacity region for all (a, b, P₁, P₂). Known: under strong interference (Sato; Han–Kobayashi 1981), to within one bit for all parameters (Etkin–Tse–Wang 2008), and the sum capacity where treating interference as noise is optimal (2008–2009); the full region under weak interference remains open.

Let G be a finite connected vertex-transitive graph with at least three vertices. Conjecture: for every geodesic (shortest path) P in G, deleting all vertices of P leaves a connected graph. Both hypotheses matter: K₂,₃ is edge-transitive and the geodesic a–x–b separates it; in the cube Q₃ a non-geodesic induced path separates it. Proposed in 2026 by Luc Gillibert; not yet studied in the literature. Left to Solve's quick computer search found no counterexample among circulant graphs on up to 18 vertices, Cayley graphs of S₃, S₄, A₄ and the dihedral groups D₅–D₈ with up to three generators, generalized Petersen graphs and Kneser graphs K(n,2), n ≤ 8.
Fair traversal conjecture (Hamiltonian paths in vertex-transitive graphs)

Conjecture: every finite connected vertex-transitive graph with at least two vertices has a nonempty finite multiset of Hamiltonian paths in which every edge occurs the same number of times (equivalently, the all-ones edge vector is a nonnegative rational combination of incidence vectors of Hamiltonian paths). It implies Lovász's conjecture that every connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamiltonian path, itself open. Proposed in 2026 by Luc Gillibert; not yet studied in the literature.

Conjecture: every finite connected vertex-transitive graph of even order can be partitioned into two nonempty vertex sets A and B such that the induced subgraphs G[A] and G[B] are connected and isomorphic. True for Cayley graphs: a fixed-point-free automorphism of order two (left multiplication by an involution of the group) yields such a partition. Open for vertex-transitive graphs that are not Cayley graphs (the Petersen graph splits into its outer 5-cycle and inner pentagram). Proposed in 2026 by Luc Gillibert; not yet studied in the literature.

Is there a topological space of cardinality $\kappa$ containing all metric spaces of cardinality $\kappa$?

It is known that all the countable metrizable spaces embed in $\mathbb{Q}$. Then a natural question is: are there an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ and a topological space $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$ such that all metrizable spaces of cardinality $\kappa$ embed in $X$?

Because there are exactly $2^\kappa$ pairwise non-homeomorphic metrizable topologies on any infinite cardinal $\kappa$, I can't disprove the existence of such a topological space by a simple size argument. My guess is that it is either independent of ZFC or it is provably false for all cardinals of size at least $2^{\aleph_0}$, using some notion of path-connectivity.

Edit: By the Kowalski's theorem, any space with a basis of cardinality $\kappa$, so notably any space of cardinality $\kappa$, can be embedded in the product of countably many $\kappa$-Hedgehog spaces. There is a simple proof of this theorem based mostly on the fact that any metrizable space has a $\sigma$-discrete basis. Hence, we have a positive answer for all cardinals $\kappa$ such that $\kappa^{\aleph_0} = \kappa$. The question is still open for the other cardinals. Thanks to Henno Brandsma for making me aware of this result.

$$\begin{matrix}\mathbb N^2 & {\huge{-\!\!\!-}} & \mathbb Z^2 \\ \huge| & {\huge\diagup}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!{\huge\diagdown} & \huge| \\ \mathbb N & {\huge{-\!\!\!-}} & \mathbb Z\end{matrix}$$

Characterization of Sequences with Integral Binomial Coefficients

For any sequence of positive integers $\{ a_i \}_{i \ge 1}$ we can define the generalized binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{k}_{a}$ as follows: 
$$m!_a = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_m, \binom{n}{k}_a = \frac{n!_a}{k!_a (n-k)!_a}$$

When $\{ a_i \}$ is a strong divisibility sequence, i.e. $\gcd (a_n, a_m) = a_{\gcd(n,m)}$, it can be shown that those coefficients are always integral, see this paper by Ward.

The problem is that this is only a sufficient condition, and I am looking for a neccesary condition.

Why is it only sufficient?

• Because it proves a stronger reuslt, namely that $\binom{n+1}{k+1}_a$ can be written as a linear integral combination of $\binom{n}{k+1}_a, \binom{n}{k}_a$.

• There are examples that don't satisfy the conditions but give integral coefficients, for example: $a_n = \binom{n+c}{c+1}$ for $c \ge 1$, see this thesis. Note that $(a_2, a_3) = (c+2, \frac{(c+3)(c+2)}{2})\ge \frac{c+2}{2} > 1$, yet $a_{(2,3)}=a_1 = 1$.
